gist: Nations are too big to feel. Let regions of a few million people steer their own life and land.
Population piles up in a few giants while the land empties. Spread towns of every size across the whole region.
City swallows country until neither is near. Interlock them as fingers, so farmland and street stay in reach.
The best soil sits in valleys, exactly where building is easiest. Keep valleys for farming; build on the slopes.
Suburbs smear town over country. Let houses gather loosely along country lanes, fields showing between.
Small towns wither as the cities pull. Give country towns their own work and reasons to stay.
Fenced-off countryside belongs to no one who walks it. Treat the land as a commons people may cross and tend.
Big cities grind difference smooth. Let many small subcultures live side by side, each with ground of its own.
Work exiled to districts leaves home hollow all day. Scatter workplaces through the places people live.
The city's real riches concentrate where few can reach them. Keep dense, magnetic cores within reach of everyone.
Cars win the long trip and ruin the short one. Bound small areas where feet and bikes come first.
A voice vanishes in mass government. Keep political communities small enough that one person can still be heard.
Ways of life pressed wall to wall wear each other down. Part subcultures with open land, not shared fences.
People need a patch of city they can name as theirs. Make neighborhoods small enough to know by face.
A neighborhood without an edge dissolves into the grid. Give it a boundary, crossed at gateways.
Separate transit lines don't add up to freedom. Weave them into one web where changing is easy.
Fast roads must exist, and destroy whatever they touch. Keep them to the edges of the areas they serve.
Learning locked in schools narrows to schooling. Spread it through the city — workshops, museums, masters.
Commerce clumps into centers far from daily life. Let shops settle at the natural spacing of need.
Big buses on fixed routes fail the odd, real journey. Fill the gaps with small buses that come when called.
High buildings lift people away from the life of the street. Keep dwellings within four stories of the ground.
Parking quietly eats the town it serves. Cap the land any area gives to resting cars.
Through-traffic tangles wherever roads cross freely. Carry it on parallel one-way roads that seldom meet.
Places that hold a community's memory get bulldozed like any lot. Protect sacred sites and their approaches.
Shorelines pass into private hands first. Keep every water's edge open for anyone to walk.
A town built for one age of life strands all the others. Provide settings for every stage, birth to death.
Places quietly built around one gender's day exclude half of life. Shape each place for the worlds of both.
A center placed dead-center leaves no quiet side. Set the dense nucleus off toward the liveliest edge.
Uniform density serves no one's real wants. Let density fall away in rings from each center.
Facilities scattered evenly never make a place. Cluster them into nodes a short walk apart.
People want somewhere to see and be seen. Give each community a short strolling spine.
Shops strung along traffic arteries serve cars, not people. Give shopping its own short street across the road.
Night spots scattered through town die alone. Gather the late places so the night has a heart.
Transfers punish the rider at every seam. Make interchanges tight, walkable, and ringed with small life.
Tracts of one household type breed monocultures. Mix homes for singles, families, and the old in every place.
One street-face is forced on host and hermit alike. Let homes sort themselves from loud fronts to quiet depths.
Houses in ranks face nobody. Gather a handful around common ground they hold together.
Where land runs short, detached houses waste it and towers erase it. Build rows, each with its own door and garden.
Density usually means stacking strangers. Terrace homes up a shared hill, each opening to the sky.
Old people gathered into enclaves disappear from life. Settle elders' dwellings through every neighborhood.
A workplace standing alone isolates its workers. Group workshops around shared courts and a common table.
Industry banished to the far edge severs work from town. Run it in narrow, buffered ribbons close by.
A walled university teaches only its own. Open it as a marketplace of courses anyone may enter.
Government at a distance goes deaf. Give each small community a town hall of its own, close to daily paths.
Civic energy dies waiting for permission and rent. String cheap ground for community projects around the hall.
A market under one owner flattens to a store. Roof over many tiny shops, each stall its own master.
Medicine waits at the end of sickness. Make health places that teach and keep people well.
Districts of pure work fall dead at night. Thread dwellings between the workplaces.
Straight residential streets invite through-traffic. Loop the local roads so only neighbors bother.
Crossroads multiply the ways two cars can meet. Join minor roads in staggered T's.
Local streets don't need a river of asphalt. Set paving stones in grass and let the street be ground.
Paths shadowing every road give walkers fumes and fear. Run paths as their own net, crossing roads at right angles.
You should feel it when you enter a community. Mark each way in with a gateway.
Crossings are drawn for the car's convenience. Raise and narrow them so walkers cross on their own terms.
Fast roads shove walkers into the gutter. Lift the walk above the roadway where the two must share.
Cycling fails without its own ways and a place at the door. Weave bike paths through, racks at every goal.
The city is built as if children didn't live there. Open safe ways for them through its real life.
A town with no license for madness goes grim. Keep ground where carnival can happen.
Work pressed against noise never rests. Give buildings quiet backs onto green, away from the street.
A green too far away might as well not exist. Put open grass within a few minutes of every door.
Vast plazas make a crowd feel like nobody. Keep public squares small enough to feel peopled.
People climb to take in their world whole. Keep a few high places to look out from.
Music and dancing retreat indoors and behind tickets. Raise bandstands where anyone may join the dance.
The city's water runs buried in pipes. Bring streams and pools back where people can touch them.
Birth happens far away, managed among strangers. Make places to be born within the community's own life.
The sacred exposed all at once is cheapened. Approach holy ground through nested thresholds.
All-private lots leave nowhere to be together. Hold common land between the houses.
A child alone in a fenced yard has no one to play with. Link the play spaces so children can find each other.
Outdoors there is nowhere to linger without buying. Build a roofed open room that belongs to everyone.
Death is removed from town until it seems not to happen. Weave small grave sites into the community's ground.
Swimming means a drive and a fee. Keep still water near home, its edge graded from paddling to depth.
Exercise exiled to stadiums becomes a spectacle. Sprinkle courts and pools where people already pass.
A finished playground leaves nothing to do. Give children raw ground and loose stuff to build with.
Towns scrubbed clean of animals teach that life is elsewhere. Make room for beasts in the ordinary fabric.
The nuclear household stands alone against everything. House larger constellations of lives together.
One open plan grinds parents and children together. Give each their realm, with a commons between.
A couple's house is more than a shared bedroom. Make one realm together and room to be apart.
A person alone needs little space but all of life in it. Make one room grown rich — alcoves for each act.
No one can settle in rooms they may not touch. Give every household a home of its own to alter.
Work under absent owners deadens the day. Favor workshops and offices the workers own and run.
Services swell into bureaucracies that serve themselves. Break them into small teams facing their people.
Groups that must work together drift when floors apart. Place connected offices within a short walk.
Telling is a poor way to learn a craft. Arrange work so beginners labor beside masters.
Teenagers are parked in classrooms at the edge of life. Give them real roles and a society of their own.
Small children vanish into big remote schools. Keep their schools tiny — a few rooms on an ordinary street.
Every child sometimes needs a household not their own. Keep a homelike refuge open in each neighborhood.
Chain shops repeat the same face everywhere. Favor shops whose owner stands behind the counter.
The street has no front porch. Let cafes spill their tables onto the walk.
Daily essentials sit a drive away. Keep a grocery on the corner, at walking distance.
Strangers need a loud warm room to drink and sing in. Keep a public hall where the whole town mixes.
Travelers are warehoused in numbered cells. Make inns where guests share the fire and the table.
Waiting at a bare pole is a small daily insult. Make each bus stop a little place — bench, shelter, news.
Eating in the street is treated as disorder. Set food stands where the paths cross.
Falling asleep in public is treated as a crime. Make spots where a nap is safe and carries no shame.
One big box swallows every function whole. Break large programs into a family of small linked buildings.
Height chosen by ego or economics ignores the town. Keep buildings low, their stories in step with the four-story limit.
A skin of parked cars deadens any building. Tuck parking behind or beneath, never facing the life.
In a maze of corridors nobody knows where they are. Nest movement into named realms, each with one clear door.
A complex of equals has no heart. Let one building stand as the head among the others.
Buildings fed by corridors turn their backs on the world. Serve them from outdoor streets instead.
A building the public must cross should not feel private. Make its passage a real street under a roof.
A row of doors, and no telling which is whose. Shape entrances as a visible family, alike and distinct.
Seas of parking repel every other use. Break lots into pockets of a handful of cars, screened by green.
Builders seize the loveliest spot and destroy it by building there. Build on the worst ground and heal it.
Outdoor land north of a building lives in its shadow. Keep the open space to the south, the building behind.
Space left over between buildings belongs to no one. Shape the outdoors as rooms with a form of their own.
Deep buildings go dark and dead at the core. Build in narrow wings so daylight reaches every room.
Slivers of space between buildings are dead on arrival. Let buildings join walls and share their edges.
A compact plan crowds everyone onto one spot. Stretch the small house long and thin, rooms in a chain.
A hidden entrance makes every arrival a search. Give the building one main door, plain from the approach.
Front gardens are display; back gardens, exile. Set the garden half-hidden at the side, private but alive.
Street to front door in one step jars the arrival. Interpose a passage of changed light, level, and view.
The car arrives at a tacked-on slab. Make the drive-up a real part of the house's entrance.
Outdoor spaces exposed on all sides give no rest. Give each a back, opening toward some larger space.
Sealed courtyards go silent and unused. Give courts a path through, a view out, and the sun.
One flat lid makes a building read as a box. Step the roofs down in a cascade from the tallest heart.
A roof hidden behind parapets shelters no one's heart. Let the roof show, and bring its edges low.
Flat roofs hold acres of unused sky. Make some of them gardens people walk out onto.
The building's edge sheds both rain and people. Run arcades along it, a public path under cover.
Paths drawn on plans get cut across on foot. Lay paths between the goals people actually walk.
A path that is only a channel forbids stopping. Swell it in the middle where people can pause.
Buildings set back behind lawns quit the street. Bring their fronts to the path, each one its own.
An empty plaza depresses; a packed one repels. Size public ground so a modest crowd makes it live.
A public space lives or dies at its rim. Ring it with pockets of activity facing in.
People perch where they can watch the passing scene. Make broad steps that face the action.
An empty middle gives no reason to stay. Put something rough at the center to gather around.
One flat plan dumps guests into private depths. Grade the rooms from public front to intimate back.
Main rooms facing away from the sun stay cold all day. Put the daily rooms on the building's bright side.
A common room at the end of a corridor stays empty. Put shared space at the crossing of everyone's paths.
Arrival deserves more than a door in a wall. Make the entrance a room, half inside and half out.
Corridors move bodies and kill encounters. Let rooms open into rooms, movement passing through life.
Long dim passages oppress everyone who walks them. Keep passages short, daylit, and wide as rooms.
A stair shut in a shaft is only plumbing for people. Open it to the room — every descent an entrance.
A view stared at all day goes stale. Reveal the best view briefly, at a turn, in passing.
Uniform brightness flattens a building's inner life. Alternate pools of light with darker ground between.
A marriage squeezed into a bedroom thins out. Give the couple a realm of the house that is theirs.
Children fitted into adult rooms are always trespassing. Give them a territory running from bed to outdoors.
Waking against the light leaves the body behind the day. Place beds where morning sun can reach them.
The cook is exiled to a galley while life happens elsewhere. Make one big room where cooking and living share.
Indoors you miss the street; on the street you have no seat. Make a half-private terrace beside the life.
No one can be shared all day long. Give each member of the household a room of their own, however small.
One sitting room must serve every mood, and serves none. Scatter sitting places from formal to nook.
A child alone behind a bedroom door is far away. Cluster children's beds in alcoves off a shared space.
Bathing is chopped into hurried utility stalls. Make one generous room for water, steam, and bodies.
Every household hauls bulky things with nowhere to keep them. Build real storage for the big stuff.
Office walls freeze yesterday's org chart. Make workspace that regroups as easily as the teams do.
Without a common table there is no common life. Make shared meals the regular heart of any group.
People massed in open halls go numb. Let work happen in groups of a handful, each with its own place.
Arrival meets a barrier manned by a gatekeeper. Make reception a hearth — warm, seated, unhurried.
Waiting rooms hold people hostage to a clock. Fold waiting into life — a window, a cafe, something to watch.
Big rooms breed big, dull meetings. Make most meeting places small enough for real talk.
A sealed office isolates; an open desk exposes. Give workers rooms half open to the flow.
A house sized for one moment of life goes obsolete. Build in rooms that can be let out or taken back.
A teenager has outgrown the nest but not the family. Give them a cottage-room at the household's edge.
The old must choose between dependence and distance. Build small cottages right beside the family house.
Work that discards its elders wastes their ripeness. Let work deepen with age into something one keeps.
Work banished from home becomes invisible to children. Keep a workshop where the house meets the street.
One internal stair makes every upstairs tenant a lodger. Give upper rooms their own open stairs from outside.
A room lit from one side glares and shadows every face. Give each room daylight from two directions.
An edge that is only a line repels lingering. Thicken the building's edge into a place to inhabit.
The sunny spot outside goes to waste without a reason to sit. Make the sun's place a destination.
The north side of a building breeds damp and gloom. Slope it low, and give it the uses that need no sun.
A garden with no walls cannot hold a gathering. Build an outdoor room — enclosed, part-roofed, open-aired.
A street no window watches feels abandoned. Let rooms lean out and keep an eye on the passing life.
Sealed frontages make the street a corridor of strangers. Open ground floors directly to the walk.
Inside and outside meet at a hard line. Wrap the building in galleries where the two mix.
A narrow balcony is a shelf nobody uses. Make balconies deep enough to hold a table and two chairs.
A house hovering above its site never touches down. Step the building to the soil in terraces and thresholds.
Grading a slope flat erases the land's form. Terrace the hillside and let building follow its lines.
Ornamental planting feeds no one. Plant fruit trees where their harvest falls into common hands.
Trees planted as decoration stand apart from life. Shape the places under and among them for people.
A manicured garden enslaves its keeper. Let the garden grow half wild, tended but not tamed.
A garden open to every noise never rests. Wall it, and pierce the wall with openings.
A bare path offers no reason to walk slowly. Build trellised walks where vines make the roof.
Garden and house meet only through a door. Add a glass room where warmth and growing things overlap.
A garden with no still corner is never truly entered. Place one quiet seat where a person can sit alone.
Food comes from nowhere anyone has seen. Keep a vegetable plot within every household's reach.
Waste flushed away breaks the soil's cycle. Return what rots to the ground that feeds you.
One open room forces everyone into one activity. Carve small alcoves off it where two can withdraw.
People drift to windows, then find no reason to stay. Make the window itself a place to inhabit.
Heat without flame gathers no one. Keep a fire as the live center the household circles.
Meals eaten under a flat glare scatter quickly. Set a heavy table in its own pool of light.
An exposed desk distracts; a closed cell entombs. Wrap each workspace in half-open enclosure.
A kitchen laid out by diagram makes the cook trek. Ring stove, sink, and counter within a step of each other.
Chairs backed against the walls kill conversation. Draw seats into a rough circle, partly enclosed.
Sleep is rationed one room per person, always apart. Make it possible to sleep near others without shame.
The marriage bed is bought as furniture. Build it as a place — enclosed, particular, the couple's own.
A whole room spent on a bed serves the bed, not sleep. Tuck the bed into an alcove scaled to it.
Dressing happens in the leftover corners of bedrooms. Give it a lit niche of its own between bed and bath.
One ceiling height flattens every social shade. Vary heights with the intimacy of the rooms.
Clever geometries fight the body's sense of shelter. Keep rooms roughly rectangular, ceilings gently vaulted.
A window onto a blank wall wastes the gaze. Aim windows at life — street, garden, coming and going.
A full wall seals rooms apart; none at all merges them. Build half-open walls that join while dividing.
Inner rooms go blind without borrowed light. Cut windows between rooms as well as to the world.
Stairs squeezed to a code minimum pinch the whole house. Give the staircase a volume it can live in.
A door in mid-wall shreds the room with paths. Hang doors near corners, leaving the body of the room whole.
Thin walls hold nothing and belong to no one. Thicken them until they carry shelves, seats, and sills.
Storage lands wherever plans have slack. Use closets as thick, quieting walls between rooms.
Counter work in shadow makes the kitchen a chore. Run the working counter along the sunny wall.
Things sealed in cupboards disappear from use. Keep the daily things on open shelves, one row deep.
The small stuff of the day needs a landing place. Run a waist-high shelf around the room's edge.
Loose chairs pushed to the wall never invite. Build seats into the fabric at the natural resting spots.
Children crave small dark dens adults can't enter. Leave cave-like spaces built at their scale.
A home with no hiding place keeps no secrets. Leave one concealed spot for the things that matter most.
Structure imposed first squeezes life into its grid. Let the social spaces come first and the frame follow.
A skeleton with cladding hung on it wastes both. Let the walls and vaults themselves do the carrying.
Industrial materials resist the hand and age badly. Build with stuff that is good to touch and easy to mend.
A building can't be perfected on paper first. Raise a light frame, then stiffen it step by step as you build.
Roofs drawn after the plan end up fighting it. Lay out the roofs with the wings, as one act.
Floors poured as abstract slabs ignore the rooms below. Shape each floor and ceiling to the spaces it covers.
A wall that is only a skin can hold no places. Thicken the outer walls as you build the alcoves into them.
A room's corners are where its loads want to land. Set columns at the corners of every social space.
A uniform grid of columns ignores how load gathers. Set them closer on the lower floors, which carry the most.
A column meeting loose ground wanders and cracks. Root each one into its own footing like a tooth.
Deep foundations cost more than the rooms above. Float the ground floor on a simple ballasted slab.
Solid columns are heavy, costly, and mute. Build hollow box columns you can fill and shape on site.
Walls meeting roof need a continuous collar. Run a perimeter beam around every floor and eave.
Walls stacked as heavy block are dead weight. Build them as two skins filled to become one membrane.
Flat spans demand steel and heavy beams. Span floors as shallow vaults that carry load by shape.
Roof shapes get chosen like hats, by fashion. Vault the roof along the lines the forces actually take.
Standard openings ignore what each room needs. Place and size every door and window where life asks.
A high sill cuts the seated off from the ground outside. Bring sills low so the world stays in view.
Glass flush in a thin wall makes a harsh bright hole. Set windows deep, with splayed reveals to soften light.
Every threshold crossed at full stride feels the same. Make doorways to intimate places low enough to notice.
Frames tacked on as trim split from the wall. Make each frame by thickening the wall's own edge.
A thin freestanding column is an obstacle. Make columns thick enough to lean against — small places.
The joint is where column and beam want to fail. Thicken the connections with braces and capitals.
A stair needs support without a cage around it. Carry it on a vault and keep the space beneath.
Services buried in the structure fail out of reach. Run ducts in open chases you can always get at.
Blown air heats the room and leaves the body cold. Warm with surfaces that shine their heat on skin.
Under a plain roof the attic stays dark and dead. Punch dormers through so the roof space becomes rooms.
A roof that just stops meets the sky abruptly. Finish its edges and ridges with caps that mark the meeting.
One flooring everywhere says every room is the same. Change the floor from hard public to soft private ground.
Flush outer skins let water find every seam. Lap the outside materials like scales, always shedding down.
Hard cold inner surfaces keep the hand away. Finish rooms in soft warm coats that take the touch.
A sealed pane turns the world into weatherproof TV. Fit windows that swing their whole frame open.
A blind door divides; a glass one fails to shelter. Make doors solid, with a glazed eye to see through.
Raw sun through plate glass glares and burns. Filter the light at its edge — vines, lattice, small panes.
One big sheet of glass flattens the world to a picture. Divide the window into small panes that bring it near.
Where materials meet, raw joints open and crack. Cover the meeting lines with simple, honest trim.
Benches placed by diagram sit empty. Put seats exactly where sun, view, and passing life converge.
The threshold invites lingering but offers no seat. Put a bench at the front door, half in the street's life.
A fence only divides. Build low walls wide enough to sit on, so the boundary gathers people.
Hard materials can't make soft, movable shade. Use canvas — awnings and roofs that open with the season.
Flowers at ground level pass underfoot unseen. Raise them in beds and pots to sill and hand height.
A bare new wall stands apart from its ground. Let climbing plants knit the building into the place.
Sealed paving kills the ground beneath it. Lay stones with earth in the cracks, so life comes through.
Hard glazed surfaces refuse the print of use. Fire soft tile and brick that wear smooth underfoot.
Decoration sprayed anywhere cheapens what it touches. Put ornament at the seams, where things meet.
Cool tones drain a room even in full sun. Choose colors that make the light itself feel warm.
Matching chair sets pretend all bodies are alike. Gather different chairs, each right for someone.
Uniform lighting flattens a room to a diagram. Hang low lamps that make pools of light over each place.
Decor bought to impress says nothing about you. Keep the things your own life has marked and made dear.
